Write a LinkedIn post based on the article below. Use your judgment about the angle, voice, length, structure and ending.

<constraints>
- Return plain prose without hashtags, emojis, decorative symbols, headings, bold text, bullet points or numbered lists.
- Avoid successive isolated one-sentence paragraphs and sequences of clipped sentences or fragments used for drama. An occasional short sentence is fine when it serves the point.
- State claims directly. Avoid rhetorical reframing such as "This isn't X; it's Y," "X, not Y," and "not X, but Y." Keep necessary factual distinctions.
- State additional capabilities directly, without "not just X," "not only X" or "more than just X" constructions.
- Omit interchangeable slogans, generic scene-setting, teaser questions and labels announcing an insight, such as "Here's the thing," "The real story," or "The takeaway?" Start with the substance.
- Replace generic benefit claims and inflated significance with the actual change or consequence. Avoid promises to "unlock potential," "transform everything" or "change the game."
- Use plain words and direct verbs. Avoid prestige vocabulary, corporate jargon and noun-heavy phrases when ordinary wording says the same thing.
- Connect ideas through their actual relationship. Avoid stock pivots such as "But here's the catch," "Let that sink in," or "And that's where things get interesting."
- Avoid invented objections, staged revelations and claims that a point is "honest," "uncomfortable" or "what nobody is talking about."
- Do not force ideas into groups of three, matching sentence templates, decorative "from X to Y" ranges or repeated short payoff lines. Let the content determine the rhythm.
- Avoid trailing significance clauses such as ", highlighting the importance of..." or ", underscoring the need for..." State a useful point directly or omit it.
- Keep uncertainty where it is needed, without stacked hedges, repeated qualifications or intensifiers added for emphasis.
- Avoid recap endings, universal lessons, generic predictions and requests for reactions such as "Thoughts?" or "Agree?" Stop when the post has said what it needs to say.
- Do not invent personal experiences, testing, conversations, emotions or discovery stories for the person publishing the post.
- Avoid repeated em dashes, ellipses, exclamation marks or rhetorical questions used to manufacture suspense or emphasis.
</constraints>

<linkedin_post>Publicly available research can still be difficult to reuse. Datasets, models and code may sit in incompatible systems or lack the documentation and provenance needed to understand them.

Project ProtoStar aims to address that gap by helping research organizations share suitable scientific resources in formats that researchers and AI systems can use. Its open challenges will also test what makes those resources practical to combine and extend.

The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University from November 2–13, uses historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Teams will predict conditions for 2019–2026 using records through 2018, then compare their forecasts with observed weather and simple baselines such as historical averages and linear trends.

That comparison gives participants a useful standard: whether an AI model improves on methods that are much simpler to use. Final forecasting results are expected in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.</linkedin_post>

<linkedin_post>Documentation shapes whether open scientific data can be used. According to the Project ProtoStar announcement, 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face come from fully documented datasets.

That matters for publicly funded research, where a dataset can be accessible online yet still be hard to interpret without clear metadata, provenance and instructions for reuse. Researchers may also need to work across incompatible systems and older file formats.

ProtoStar brings universities, research organizations and industry together to encourage the release of suitable datasets, models and code in machine-actionable formats. Its planned challenges will use those resources to identify documentation gaps and technical barriers that make reuse difficult.

Carnegie Mellon University’s first challenge, running November 2–13, asks teams to forecast urban climate conditions using historical weather data. Participants will compare their predictions against observed conditions and statistical baselines, and propose a climate adaptation policy idea informed by the data.</linkedin_post>

<linkedin_post>Research teams have shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as they did in the same period of 2025. The growth remained substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Making those resources useful takes work beyond publishing the files. Researchers need enough information to understand how data was produced, what it contains and how it can be reused alongside other work.

Project ProtoStar aims to support that work through publishing guidance, open infrastructure and a series of challenges hosted by research institutions. The challenges will give participants a chance to build with openly released scientific resources while identifying gaps in documentation and compatibility.

Carnegie Mellon University is hosting the first challenge from November 2–13, focused on predicting urban climate conditions using historical weather records.</linkedin_post>

<linkedin_post>Carnegie Mellon University’s Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge will test AI forecasts against a useful benchmark: how well they predict weather conditions that have already been observed.

Teams will use records through 2018 for 210 U.S. cities to forecast annual temperature, precipitation, the hottest day of the year and cooling degree days for 2019–2026. Their results will be compared with historical averages and linear trends, making it possible to see whether the added complexity improves accuracy.

The challenge runs November 2–13 as the first in Project ProtoStar’s open science series. Participants will also propose a climate adaptation policy idea based on their analysis. Final forecasting results are expected in early 2027, after the complete 2026 weather records become available.</linkedin_post>
